design_detail: Single-centre, open-label randomized crossover trial with matched triplets (Witten/Herdecke University, Germany, summer 2017): participants matched on age, sex, body size, drinking and hangover frequency were randomized 1:1:1 to beer then wine (study group 1), wine then beer (study group 2), or a control group drinking only beer or only wine, each to the same breath alcohol target, under medical supervision with an overnight stay; in a second session each person drank in the opposite order (or the other single drink); targets and intervals are in the exposure field. Primary outcome: Acute Hangover Scale the next day; 90 of 105 randomized completed.
can_establish: Whether drinking beer before wine, rather than wine before beer, to the same supervised level of intoxication changes next-day hangover severity by as much as the trial's prespecified difference (about 8 points on a 0 to 56 scale) in healthy young adults.
cannot_establish: Whether order makes a smaller difference (the interval of the primary comparison runs to about 4 points either way; editors' calculation), whether other drinks (spirits, red wine, dark beer) behave differently, whether results hold for unsupervised drinking without water before bed, and whether vomiting or feeling very drunk cause worse hangovers (they are exploratory correlates that are part of the same heavy intoxication).

sample.recruitment: Volunteers from Witten/Herdecke University recruited by an online survey, September 2016 to June 2017; interventions 1 July to 26 August 2017.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Aged 18 to 60, drinking both beer and wine, physically fit, with two available matching partners. Excluded: aversion to beer or wine, history of drug or alcohol abuse, abstinence or alcohol intolerance, East Asian origin (because of common variants of alcohol-metabolizing genes), abnormal liver tests or liver disease, viral hepatitis, chronic pain, epilepsy, Wernicke or Korsakoff syndrome, thiamine deficiency, gastritis, bariatric surgery, immunosuppression, recent infection, pregnancy or breastfeeding, frequent use of pain medication, and medications that interact with alcohol (for example antibiotics, opioids, nitrates, antidepressants).
sample.demographics: Age 19 to 40 (group means 23.6 to 24.3); 48.4%, 48.4% and 53.6% women; mean BMI about 22.3; drinking several times a month and hangovers between rarely and a few times a month in all groups (Table 1).
sample.attrition: 105 randomized, 90 completed (14% lost), mostly because the trial overlapped with exams or holidays; if a study-group member dropped out, the whole matched triplet was excluded; per-protocol analysis. The target of 36 per study group was not reached.
sample.selection_effects: Young, healthy university volunteers who drink both beer and wine and could be matched; completers only.

exposure.measurement: Supervised drinking with breath alcohol measured hourly (AlcoQuant 6020+, after 15 minutes without food or drink) and again the next morning; readings were not shown to participants. The drink of the day was disclosed only on the evening of each session.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: Carlsberg 1847 Pilsner lager (5%) and a 2015 white wine (Chasselas/Johanniter, 11.1%), served cold. Study groups drank the first drink to a breath alcohol of 0.05% or more, then the second to 0.11% (switch at about 0.06%, after 1.7 to 2.3 hours); about 1.2 to 1.4 L of beer and 0.6 to 0.7 L of wine per session; peak breath alcohol 0.12 to 0.13% in all groups after about 3.6 to 4.6 hours; controls drank about 2.6 L of beer or 1.2 L of wine (Table 2). Drinking could stop early at the person's wish or for safety. A standardized meal before drinking, 6 mL/kg of water before sleep, and an overnight stay under medical supervision; no alcohol for one week before each session. The second session was at least one week after the first.
exposure.polysubstance: Medications interacting with alcohol and frequent pain medication excluded; smoking and other drug use not reported.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Hangover rated the next day once breath alcohol had returned to zero.

comparison.controls: Within person: the same participants drinking in the opposite order in a second session. A parallel control group drank one beverage only on each day.
comparison.matching: Triplets matched on age, sex, weight, height, BMI, drinking frequency and hangover frequency (Supplemental Table 1, not read), each triplet randomized with a six-sided die.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not relevant within person; sleep duration was described as similar but not measured.

outcomes.instruments: Acute Hangover Scale as an 8-item compound score (thirst, fatigue, headache, dizziness, nausea, stomach ache, racing heart, loss of appetite), each 0 to 7, total 0 to 56; perceived drunkenness 0 to 10 at the end of drinking; vomiting; blood and urine tests before drinking and the next day (Supplemental Table 3, not read).
outcomes.validity_norms: The scale is cited to its developers; Rohsenow et al. (2014, read in this round) describe the Acute Hangover Scale as nine items including an overall hangover item, while this trial used eight.
outcomes.operationalization: Primary: the within-person difference in hangover score between the two drinking orders, compared between study group 1 and study group 2 (Welch two-sample t test); the defining formula is printed as an image.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. One primary comparison; secondary analyses (sex, relative score per unit of peak breath alcohol, a cluster analysis, regression with backward selection on both days, laboratory panels) are numerous and several are reported as data not shown, so the number of tests cannot be counted.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: None: open label. The authors say blinding beer and wine proved impossible in a pre-trial, and that an alcohol-free control was not feasible.

analysis.effect_sizes: Primary: within-person difference X in study group 1 −0.32 (SD 7.63) against Y in study group 2 0.36 (SD 6.82), P = 0.71 (editors' approximate 95% CI for X minus Y −4.4 to 3.0 points on the 0 to 56 scale). No group differed in hangover score between its two days (P > 0.05; control group beer-only against wine-only days included). Period difference ('carryover' test) P = 0.8. Women reported more severe hangovers than men (P = 0.009, data not shown), not significant after dividing by peak breath alcohol. Vomiting and perceived drunkenness were associated with higher scores on both days in regression (coefficients in Figure 5, an image; values not extracted).
analysis.covariates: Exploratory regression with backward selection by Akaike information criterion, with unadjusted 95% CIs; 89 participants on day 1 and 88 on day 2.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Approved beforehand by the Witten/Herdecke University Ethics Committee (140/2016), which the authors call prospective registration, and registered in the German Clinical Trials Register (DRKS00015285) only retrospectively. No public prospective registration, so the primary analysis cannot be checked against a protocol.
analysis.selective_reporting: Mean hangover scores for each condition are not given in text or tables (box plots only); the sex difference, the cluster analysis and some regressions are reported as data not shown; individual symptoms are in a supplement not read.
analysis.power: Planned for 36 per study group to detect a 14% difference (1 point per item, about 8 points) with 80% power at 5%; 31 per group completed. The observed interval excludes a difference of 8 points (editors' calculation).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 62 young adults who drank beer and wine in both orders to the same breath alcohol, the order did not detectably change next-day hangover severity (difference between groups −0.68 points on a 0 to 56 scale, editors' 95% CI about −4.4 to 3.0, P = 0.71), and controls did not differ between a beer-only and a wine-only day. Differences as large as the trial's planned 8 points are excluded; smaller ones are not. In exploratory regressions, vomiting and feeling drunk went with worse hangovers; women reported worse hangovers than men.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says the findings "dispel the traditional myths" and the Discussion that they "debunk" them, and the authors advise readers to heed perceived drunkenness and vomiting to reduce hangover intensity. Gaps: (1) one trial with lager and white wine, open label and per protocol, cannot debunk an effect smaller than about 4 points or with other drinks; (2) vomiting and perceived drunkenness are markers of the same heavy intoxication, found by backward selection in exploratory models, and are not shown to be causes that can be acted on; (3) the Discussion states that women and men did not differ in hangover severity, while the Results report that women's hangovers were more severe (P = 0.009).

timeline.event: This trial: by the authors' account the first data to test the beer-and-wine order sayings.

replication.where_it_stands: The only randomized test of drink order and hangover; its null result is reasonably precise for large differences, for lager and white wine at the level of intoxication studied.

funding.funder: No external funding is stated; Carlsberg donated the beer free of charge and, per the paper, had no role in design, conduct or analysis.
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors report no conflicts of interest related to the research.
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from Witten/Herdecke University and HELIOS University Hospital Wuppertal.

what_would_settle_it: A preregistered randomized crossover replication at another centre with blinded outcome assessment where possible, more drink types (spirits, red wine, dark beer), more than one level of intoxication, realistic bedtimes without supplied water, prespecified secondary analyses, and full reporting of mean hangover scores by condition.

domains.note: Matched triplets randomized with a die and the drink of the day concealed until the evening; study groups balanced at baseline (Table 1). In the control group, 7 of 28 drank beer first and 21 wine first, which is unlikely under a 1:1 random choice (two-sided binomial p about 0.01; editors' calculation) and is not explained, but the control group is not part of the primary comparison.

domains.domain: Bias arising from period and carryover effects (crossover)
domains.note: Washout and abstinence before each session (intervals in the exposure field); no difference between study days (P = 0.8).
Supervised drinking to breath alcohol targets with an overnight stay; open label, but no sign of departures from the assigned order.
15 of 105 randomized (14%) not analysed, mostly for exams or holidays; whole triplets were excluded when a study-group member dropped out.

Self-rated hangover by participants who knew what they drank and in what order; the folk sayings are well known, but both sequences involved mixing, and expectation would favour the saying rather than the null result.
Only retrospective public registration; condition means are not reported numerically and several secondary results are data not shown.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: A well-controlled supervised design with matched randomization and within-person comparison; the concerns are open-label self-rating, per-protocol analysis with 14% loss, and retrospective registration with incomplete numerical reporting. The card may be cited for no detectable effect of the order of beer and wine on next-day hangover at the amounts and drinks studied, with differences as large as the planned 8 points excluded. It should not be cited for vomiting or perceived drunkenness as causes of hangover, nor as showing no sex difference.

key_findings.finding: Primary endpoint: the within-person difference in Acute Hangover Scale score between drinking orders was −0.32 (SD 7.63) in study group 1 and 0.36 (SD 6.82) in study group 2, P = 0.71; no group's score differed between its two days.
key_findings.locator: Results › Alcohol-induced hangover intensity, 2nd paragraph; Figure 3
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: X minus Y = −0.68 points, approximate 95% CI −4.4 to 3.0 on the 0 to 56 scale; the planned difference was about 8 points (1 point on each of 8 items).

key_findings.finding: Control participants did not differ in hangover between a beer-only and a wine-only day (P > 0.05); 7 of 28 drank beer on day 1 and 21 wine.

Drinking conditions were comparable: breath alcohol at the switch and at its peak was similar in all sequences and groups (values in the exposure field); the switch came sooner when wine was drunk first.
key_findings.locator: Table 2; Results › Trial progress specifics, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Dividing each person's hangover score by his or her peak breath alcohol gave the same pattern as the uncorrected scores.
key_findings.locator: Results › Alcohol-induced hangover intensity, 3rd paragraph; Supplemental Figure 1 (not read)

key_findings.finding: Women reported more severe hangovers than men on both days (P = 0.009, data not shown); after dividing by peak breath alcohol the difference was a non-significant tendency (45 women, 45 men).
key_findings.locator: Results › Factors associated with hangover intensity, 1st paragraph; Figure 4 legend

key_findings.finding: In exploratory regressions with backward selection (89 participants on day 1, 88 on day 2), vomiting and perceived drunkenness were associated with higher hangover scores on both days; blood and urine tests did not differ between groups.
key_findings.locator: Results › Factors associated with hangover intensity, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Figure 5 legend

key_findings.finding: Vomiting occurred more often in the control group (wine only 6, beer only 5) than in the study groups (2 to 4), and in more women than men on both days (5 against 4; 8 against 4).
Of 272 screened, 247 were eligible, 105 were matched and randomized and 90 completed; the planned 36 per study group was not reached because of loss to follow-up during exams and holidays.
key_findings.locator: Results › Study population, 1st paragraph; Methods › Sample size

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion states that no difference between women and men in hangover severity was found, while the Results report more severe hangovers in women (P = 0.009), attenuated only after dividing by peak breath alcohol.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Discussion, 2nd paragraph; Results › Factors associated with hangover intensity, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The sex finding should be taken from the Results: women reported worse hangovers, partly explained by higher breath alcohol.

reporting_issues.issue: The control group is 28 in the text and Table 1 but 29 in the heading of Table 2.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 1; Table 2; Results › Study population
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor inconsistency in the denominators of the drinking data.

reporting_issues.issue: Of 28 controls, 7 were assigned beer first and 21 wine first, though assignment was described as random by die; a split this uneven has a two-sided probability of about 0.01 under a 1:1 random choice (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Randomization; Results › Alcohol-induced hangover intensity, 2nd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The control group's assignment may not have been 1:1 random; it does not affect the primary comparison.

reporting_issues.issue: What the paper calls a carryover test compares summed scores between the two days, which tests a period effect; and the Methods say it was done before the first intervention, which is not possible.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Biostatistical analyses, 3rd paragraph; Results › Alcohol-induced hangover intensity, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Carryover was not formally assessed, though the washout makes it unlikely.

reporting_issues.issue: The formula defining the primary within-person differences is printed as an image, and mean hangover scores for each drink condition are not given in text or tables.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Biostatistical analyses, equation (1); Results; Figure 3
reporting_issues.consequence: The size of hangovers in each condition cannot be quoted; only the difference statistics can.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion advises readers to heed perceived drunkenness and vomiting to reduce hangover intensity, from exploratory associations after backward model selection.
reporting_issues.consequence: A correlational, exploratory result presented as practical advice; not a finding about prevention.
